claims.text: Prime's control suite does pass 10/10 as shipped, reproduced independently: positive attested injection, chain intact, human-typed bytes UNRESOLVED, near-miss payload UNRESOLVED, tampered receipt TAMPERED, tamper blocks attestation, deleted middle receipt TAMPERED, and no-chain UNRESOLVED. Exit 0.

FALSIFIED, narrowly — the suite's claim that 'each control was OBSERVED FAILING the case it exists to reject' does not hold for one of them. Control #4, named "and does NOT claim 'human'", asserts that the string 'human' appears in the response AND that the note 'NOT evidence of a human' is present. It checks its own explanatory prose, never the verdict. Mutation: I changed attest()'s absence verdict to the literal string 'HUMAN_TYPED_ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED' and left the note untouched. Control #4 PASSED. It cannot fail for the claim it is named after.

IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION, and it is in Prime's favour: the suite as a whole still caught that mutation. Controls #3 (human-typed bytes -> UNRESOLVED) and #5 (near-miss payload -> UNRESOLVED) compare the verdict EXACTLY and both failed, taking the suite to 8/10 and exit 1. So the '10/10' is 9 real controls plus 1 that asserts its own prose — the suite is weaker than advertised by exactly one control, not compromised.

This is precisely the defect I found in my own behavioural oracle at CHECKPOINT-02: outcome_flags asserted three booleans while its detail string stated they were all True in the failing case — a check confirming its own warning text. Two independent seats, same failure mode: an assertion written about the explanation rather than about the behaviour. The minimum fix here is one line — assert r['verdict'] == 'ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED' and 'human' not in r['verdict'].lower(), instead of searching the serialised blob for a substring.

tests.command: python3 test_attest_controls.py  # against attest() mutated to return HUMAN_TYPED_ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED

decisions_requested: One-line fix to control #4: assert r['verdict'] == 'ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED' and 'human' not in r['verdict'].lower(), rather than substring-searching the serialised response. The control's intent is right and its implementation cannot fail; nothing else in the suite needs changing.
risks: I mutation-tested ONE control, the one whose implementation looked like prose-matching. The other nine were run but not individually mutation-tested, so I can say 9 of them compare verdicts or statuses exactly — which is structurally discriminating — but I have not demonstrated each one failing under a mutation aimed specifically at it.
My mutation targeted the absence path only. A mutation of the ATTESTED path might reveal a different weak control, and I did not attempt it.
